english.html: who presently gives something swears to keep his liberality and not to contravene what he promises and gives; but he who acknowledges and swears to have long since received some sum of money or other thing interposes his oath upon what is already done and past, that is to say, upon what has already before been received by the acknowledger.

notes.original: Bartole en la l. quis pro eo D. de fideiuſſo.

english.html: Afterwards he institutes as his heiress his daughter Bernarde du Tilh, whom he had had of the said Bertrande de Rols; and gives her as guardians Jean du Tilh his brother, inhabitant of Le Pin, and Dominique Rebendaire, inhabitant of Toulouse.

A fine question presents itself here: whether this institution of an heir is valid, and so whether a man condemned to death can make a testament. And although such a dispute may seem to many to be without difficulty, because our Jurisconsults, and with them Justinian, teach in divers places that testaments already made are quashed and broken by the condemnation to death that follows — so far is it from the condemned man's being able to make new ones after the sentence <sup class="mk" data-key="a">a</sup> — nevertheless grave authors in our Jurisprudence relate that they have often seen testaments made by those condemned to death, but have never heard of the quashing of any <sup class="mk" data-key="b">b</sup>. Added to which, by the new constitutions of Justinian it seems that this rigour of the law, refusing to permit the condemned the faculty of making a testament, has received some change <sup class="mk" data-key="c">c</sup>, because the reason on which the interdiction of making a testament, in those condemned to death, was founded (which is that where someone was condemned to death his goods also were confiscated, and so, having no goods, he could not make a testament <sup class="mk" data-key="e">e</sup>) seems to cease today, the goods being, by the new law, exempt from confiscation and reserved to the nearest successors ab intestato, except

notes.citation: Digest 28.1 (Qui testamenta facere possunt et quemadmodum testamenta fiant; Coras's de teſta.), l. Eius § 1 and l. Si cui § 1 (cf. D. 28.1.8, Gaius, whose § 1 begins Si cui aqua et igni interdictum sit); Digest 28.3 (De iniusto rupto irrito facto testamento), l. Si quis exheredato § Irritum; Institutes 2.17 (Quibus modis testamenta infirmantur), § Alio quoque modo (Inst. 2.17.4)
notes.original: l. eius P. j. l. ſi cui. P. j. D. de teſta, l,⟨alt:l.⟩ ſi quis exheredato, P. irritũ. D. de iniuſt. te ſta. P. alio. q mol. eſt. infir.
notes.gloss: Those condemned to the sword, the beasts or the mines lose liberty and the power to make a will; a will already made becomes irritum when the testator suffers capitis deminutio. The margin's q mol. eſt. is a garbling of quomodo teſt.

notes.citation: Albericus de Rosate (Alberique) on l. Eius § Si cui (D. 28.1.8), cited above, and on the Authentica Bona damnatorum under Code 9.49 (De bonis proscriptorum seu damnatorum)
notes.original: Alberique en la l. eius, P. ſi cui, prealleguee, & en l'Auten bona C. de bon. pro ſcrip.
notes.gloss: Albericus is the "grave author" who had often seen the condemned make wills and never heard one quashed.

notes.citation: Authenticum, coll. 9, Nov. 134 (Ut nulli iudicum), last chapter (Nov. 134.13); and the Authentica Bona damnatorum under Code 9.49
notes.original: P, Dernier vt nulli iudi. coll. ix. & en l'Autent. bona.
notes.gloss: Nov. 134.13: the goods of a condemned man pass to his descendants or ascendants, not to the fisc, treason excepted — the "new constitution" of the argument.

notes.original: Autent, ingreſſi C. de ſa croſanct. eccl.
notes.gloss: Those who enter a monastery lose their goods to it, and having none cannot make a will — the parallel for the condemned.
